# Raw moment John maxima: attainment, strict interpolation, empty lattice hull, and mass stationarity

This is a theorem about a geometric source body. It does not assert that its John center has any halfspace-depth guarantee. Indeed `candidate e16770c76630ebf6` disproves such a selector inference already for intervals.

## 1. Definitions and conclusions

Let `d>=1`, let `P subset Z^n` be finite and nonempty, and let every `K_z subset R^d` be a positive-volume compact convex body. Put
\[
 \mu=\sum_{z\in P}\delta_z\otimes 1_{K_z}\,dx,\qquad M=\mu(S).
\]
For any feasible pair `b=(t,v) in R x R^n`, define the raw moment body
\[
 Q(b)=\left\{\int xf\,d\mu:0\le f\le1,
      \ \int f\,d\mu=t,\quad\int zf\,d\mu=v\right\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Feasible pairs form a compact convex set D. At a feasible integer base j write
\[
 Q_t(j)=Q(t,tj),\qquad
 T_j=\max\{t:(t,tj)\in D\}.
\]
The feasible integer bases are exactly `conv(P) intersect Z^n`, a finite set. Define
\[
 J(Q)=\max\{(\det A)^{1/d}:c+A B_d\subset Q,\ A\succeq0\},
\tag{2}
\]
where a lower-dimensional Q has value zero. Its John ellipsoid volume is `|B_d| J(Q)^d`, so maximizing (2) is equivalent to maximizing that volume.

**Theorem.** The joint maximum of `J(Q_t(j))` over feasible integers j and `0<t<=T_j` is attained and is positive. At every maximizing base its maximizing mass is unique. Let E be the set of maximizing integer bases. Then
\[
 \boxed{\quad E=\operatorname{vert}(\operatorname{conv}E),\qquad
  \operatorname{conv}E\cap\mathbb Z^n=E,\qquad |E|\le2^n.\quad}
\tag{3}
\]
Here for `n=0` there is one base and the last bound is one.

The strict-interpolation and empty-hull arguments include boundary masses `T_j` and do not assume their sections are full dimensional. Moreover, whenever j itself has a positive source fiber, its maximizing mass satisfies `0<t<T_j`, by the independent deletion argument in Section 4. Thus every integer maximizing mass is interior in the actual convex-body setting. A lower-dimensional raw section is assigned John value zero throughout; a global maximizer necessarily has positive value.

If a maximizing mass is interior, `0<t<T_j`, its John contacts can be chosen with actual source-cap duals satisfying an additional exact mass stationarity condition. In the notation proved in Section 6,
\[
 \sum_i\lambda_i b_i=0,\qquad
 \sum_i\lambda_i\Psi_i=d.
\tag{4}
\]
For an abstract source with a feasible integer base absent from P, an interior-mass assertion is not presumed; the deletion argument specifically uses a positive fiber at the selected base.

For fibers arising from an actual convex body C, every feasible integer base belongs to a positive-volume actual fiber. Indeed any convex representation of j by positive fibers supplies a positive-volume Minkowski average inside `C_j`. Thus `conv(P) intersect Z^n=P` in that setting. The theorem itself does not need convex compatibility between distinct fibers.

## 2. Compactness and the unique indicator support source, including boundary constraints

The densities `0<=f<=1` form a weak-star compact subset of `L^infinity(mu)`. Their mass and all first moments are continuous for this topology because the source is finite and bounded. Consequently D and all nonempty Q(b) are compact, and the graph `{(b,q):q in Q(b)}` is compact and convex.

Fix `u!=0`. In a single full-dimensional convex fiber, among all densities with a fixed mass `m in [0,|K_z|]`, the unique maximizer of `integral u.x f dx` is its upper u-cap of that mass (empty or full at the endpoints). Existence of a threshold for an interior mass follows from continuity and strict decrease of the volume tail between its two support levels. For its threshold a, the inequality
\[
 \int (u\cdot x-a)(1_{\{u\cdot x\ge a\}}-f)\,dx\ge0
\]
proves optimality; equality forces equality of the densities almost everywhere, since a nonzero continuous linear functional has level sets of zero volume.

It follows that a source maximizing the support of Q(b) is an indicator in every fiber: replacing just one fiber by its unique rearranged source preserves both the total mass and the integer first moment. Furthermore the global maximizing source is unique. If two distinct optimal sources existed, their average would also be optimal but would be fractional on a set of positive measure. On at least one fiber it could then be strictly improved by the preceding rearrangement, a contradiction.

This argument holds at **every feasible pair b**, including boundary pairs, `t=T_j`, completely saturated sources, and lower-dimensional Q(b). It does not require an attained finite ambient cap dual there. The maximizing indicator can have a different threshold in each fiber at a boundary constraint.

## 3. Strict interpolation of raw moment bodies

Let `b_1!=b_2` be two feasible constraint pairs, and `0<lambda<1`. Ordinary source mixing gives
\[
 \lambda Q(b_1)+(1-\lambda)Q(b_2)
 \subset Q(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)b_2).
\]
In fact there is an `epsilon>0` such that
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \lambda Q(b_1)+(1-\lambda)Q(b_2)+\epsilon B_d
 \subset Q(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)b_2).\quad}
\tag{5}
\]
To prove it, fix a unit u and let `f_1,f_2` be the unique support sources from Section 2. They are different because they satisfy different constraint pairs. Their mixed source is fractional on their positive-measure symmetric difference, so it is not the maximizing source at the mixed constraints. Hence
\[
 h_{Q(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)b_2)}(u)
 >\lambda h_{Q(b_1)}(u)+(1-\lambda)h_{Q(b_2)}(u).
\]
The difference is a continuous positive function on the compact unit sphere, since these are support functions of fixed compact bodies. Its minimum is positive, proving (5). The same argument applies directly to any finite positive mixture involving at least two different constraint pairs.

In particular the statement explicitly supplies density slack: the mixed indicator sources are genuinely fractional on positive volume and admit a *strict* improvement preserving every fiber mass. No iteration is assumed to remain dominated after its capacities change.

The John radius is consequently strictly concave in the feasible constraint pair:
\[
 J(Q(\lambda b_1+(1-\lambda)b_2))
 >\lambda J(Q(b_1))+(1-\lambda)J(Q(b_2)).
\tag{6}
\]
Here is the determinant detail. Choose maximal inscribed ellipsoids with centers `c_i` and positive semidefinite shapes `A_i`; in a degenerate body choose any point with shape zero. The left side of (5) contains the ellipsoid with center `lambda c_1+(1-lambda)c_2` and shape
`lambda A_1+(1-lambda)A_2+epsilon I`. Its determinant root is strictly larger than that of `lambda A_1+(1-lambda)A_2`, and the latter is at least the weighted sum of the two determinant roots. The determinant inequality for positive definite shapes follows by conjugating one to the identity and expanding the product in the eigenvalues of the other: each elementary symmetric mean is at least the corresponding power of their geometric mean by arithmetic–geometric mean applied to all subsets. Limits handle semidefinite shapes. Addition of `epsilon I` strictly increases the determinant root even when the unperturbed matrix is singular. This proves (6).

## 4. Positive attained maxima and harmonic interpolation of bases

For each fixed integer j, the feasible masses form `[0,T_j]`; `Q_0(j)={0}`. Upper semicontinuity of the John radius follows directly from the compact graph: along convergent pairs, centers and shapes of bounded inscribed ellipsoids have convergent subsequences, and every limit ellipsoid is contained in the limiting moment body. Determinants converge. Compactness of the mass interval and finiteness of feasible integer bases therefore give a maximum.

It is positive. For any z in P, the two pairs corresponding to the empty source and the full single-fiber source are different. Their midpoint moment body contains a ball by (5). In particular the maximizing mass is positive. Strict concavity (6) along the ray `(t,tj)` makes the maximizing mass unique at each base, including a possible maximum at the right endpoint.

There is a useful stronger boundary conclusion if `j in P`. Every maximum-mass balanced source fills the entire fiber `K_j` almost everywhere: adding any missing density on that fiber preserves its zero base moment and would increase its mass beyond `T_j`. Let `0<epsilon<|K_j|`, and let
\[
 Z_\epsilon(K_j)=\left\{\int_{K_j}x g(x)\,dx:0\le g\le1,\quad\int g=\epsilon\right\}.
\]
Subtracting any such single-fiber source from any maximum-mass source gives the exact Minkowski inclusion
\[
 \boxed{\quad Q_{T_j-\epsilon}(j)\supset Q_{T_j}(j)-Z_\epsilon(K_j).\quad}
\tag{7a}
\]
The body `Z_epsilon(K_j)` has a positive inball. Explicitly, if `theta=(epsilon/|K_j|)^(1/d)`, the homothetic sources `(1-theta)p+theta K_j`, for `p in K_j`, have volume epsilon and give the contained raw moment body
`epsilon[(1-theta)K_j+theta g_(K_j)]`. Thus adding `-Z_epsilon` strictly increases the John radius of any positive-radius ellipsoid by the determinant argument of Section 3. If the boundary radius is zero, a positive interior value already excludes it as a maximum. Consequently **the unique maximizing mass at every positive source base j lies strictly between zero and T_j**. The proof keeps all deletion densities within the original capacities and works even when Q_T itself has lower dimension.

Let `R>0` be the joint maximum. Suppose an integer point j has a nontrivial convex representation
\[
 j=\sum_{i=1}^k\rho_i j_i,\quad
 \rho_i>0,\quad\sum_i\rho_i=1,
\]
by maximizing bases with their unique positive masses `t_i`. Put
\[
 Z=\sum_i\frac{\rho_i}{t_i},\qquad
 \alpha_i=\frac{\rho_i/t_i}{Z},\qquad t_0=\frac1Z.
\tag{7}
\]
Then the source mixture has mass `sum alpha_i t_i=t_0` and base moment
`sum alpha_i t_i j_i=t_0 j`. Thus j is feasible. At least two constraint pairs are distinct, and finite-mixture strictness in (5), together with the determinant inequality, gives
\[
 J(Q_{t_0}(j))>\sum_i\alpha_i R=R,
\]
a contradiction. This excludes both an additional integer point in the convex hull and a maximizing base represented nontrivially by the others. It proves the first two assertions in (3). Two distinct maximizing bases in the same parity class have an integer midpoint represented nontrivially, so there is at most one in each of the `2^n` parity classes.

For two bases, (7) becomes exactly the unequal-mass harmonic interpolation:
\[
 \alpha_1=\frac{t_2}{t_1+t_2},\quad
 \alpha_2=\frac{t_1}{t_1+t_2},\quad
 t_0=\frac{2t_1t_2}{t_1+t_2}.
\]
Thus unequal masses and boundary capacities cause no gap in the parity argument.

## 5. Contact planes at an interior mass lift to actual ambient cap sources

Fix j and `0<t_0<T_j`. The convex joint body
\[
 \mathcal B_j=\{(t,q):0\le t\le T_j,\ q\in Q_t(j)\}
\]
has full dimension `d+1`. Every intermediate section Q is full dimensional by (5). Sections vary continuously near an interior mass: source mixing with a fixed larger-mass source or with the zero source gives lower Hausdorff convergence, while compactness of the graph gives upper convergence. Consequently if c is interior to `Q_(t_0)(j)`, then `(t_0-h,c)` and `(t_0+h,c)` belong to the joint body for all sufficiently small positive h.

A supporting plane to this joint body at `(t_0,q_0)`, with nonzero continuous normal u, can be written
\[
 u\cdot q\le u\cdot q_0+b(t-t_0).
\tag{8}
\]
Every such contact plane has an actual original-source cap representation
\[
 H=\{u\cdot x+a\cdot(z-j)-b\ge0\}
\tag{9}
\]
whose source has mass exactly `t_0`, base mean j, and raw continuous moment `q_0` if q_0 is the continuous support point.

For clarity, the coefficient b in (9) is the **same prescribed slope** as in (8). To prove attainment with that b, restrict the source to the minimal face F of `conv(P)` containing j, and restrict a to `V=span(F-j)`. Choose a uniformly fractional positive density on all fibers of F with zero base moment, using strictly positive convex coefficients representing j. Its total mass is immaterial here. It yields the coercive bound
\[
 \int(u\cdot x-b+a\cdot(z-j))_+\,d\mu_F
 \ge\delta\sum_{z\in F}w_z|a\cdot(z-j)|-C.
\]
The sum is a norm on V. Thus the expression attains a minimum in a. Nonzero u makes its level set null; differentiation gives zero source base moment. The pointwise positive-part inequality proves that this cap maximizes `integral (u.x-b)f` over all base-balanced sources of arbitrary mass. Plane (8) says its maximum is achieved by the prescribed support source at `(t_0,q_0)`. Uniqueness of that source (or the same positive-margin exchange without a mass constraint) identifies it with this cap. A sufficiently large finite exposing coefficient empties all fibers outside F, without changing b or any trace on F. This proves (9).

The boundary case `t_0=T_j` was not used here. Vertical supporting planes may then occur, and an attained finite continuous cap dual for every contact is not asserted.

## 6. Exact free-mass stationarity at John contacts

Suppose `t_0` is an interior maximizing mass at j. Write its John ellipsoid as `c+A B_d`, with `A` symmetric positive definite, and normalize raw moment coordinates by `q -> A^(-1)(q-c)`. Its section ellipsoid is the unit ball.

There exist finitely many unit contact directions `v_i`, positive weights `lambda_i`, and contact plane slopes `b_i`, such that
\[
 \sum_i\lambda_i v_i=0,\qquad
 \sum_i\lambda_i v_i v_i^T=I_d,\qquad
 \boxed{\ \sum_i\lambda_i b_i=0.\ }
\tag{10}
\]
One needs at most `1+d+d(d+1)/2` contacts.

Here is the complete extra stationarity argument. At a unit-ball contact, a joint supporting plane has continuous normal v equal to its unit contact point. No vertical supporting plane can occur because `t_0` is interior and the center remains in nearby sections. Moreover the slopes b are uniformly bounded: test the plane on `(t_0+-h,0)` to get `|b|<=1/h`. Thus all contact triples `(-b,v,vv^T)` form a compact set. Their generated cone is closed because the trace of the last component is one, bounding the total coefficient of every convergent conic sequence.

If `(0,0,I)` were outside this cone, separation would give a mass variation s, a center variation p, and a symmetric shape variation B with `tr B>0` and
\[
 -b s+v\cdot p+v^T Bv\le0
\]
for every contact. Replacing B by `B-epsilon I`, with positive trace retained, makes this strict uniformly. For small positive h, the ellipsoid of center hp and shape `I+hB` at mass `t_0+hs` stays in the joint body and has larger volume. To justify containment, use its supporting-plane characterization: directions near the compact contact set have a strictly negative first-order support change, uniformly; all other unit full supporting normals have a positive support gap at the original ball. Compactness and the uniform support expansion cover these directions simultaneously. This contradicts maximality. Hence the cone contains `(0,0,I)`. Finite-dimensional conic Caratheodory gives (10) and the stated cardinality. Taking the trace gives `sum lambda_i=d`.

Return to original raw moment coordinates and put `u_i=A^(-1)v_i`. Section 5 supplies actual ambient caps
\[
 L_i=u_i\cdot x+a_i\cdot(z-j)-b_i,\qquad
 \Psi_i=\int(L_i)_+\,d\mu,
\]
with
\[
 \mu(H_i)=t_0,\quad
 \int_{H_i}(z-j)\,d\mu=0,\quad
 \int_{H_i}x\,d\mu=c+A v_i.
\tag{11}
\]
Their exact support values are
\[
 t_0 b_i+\Psi_i=h_{Q_{t_0}(j)}(u_i)=u_i\cdot c+1.
\]
Multiply by `lambda_i`, sum, and use (10). This proves
\[
 \boxed{\ \sum_i\lambda_i\Psi_i=d.\ }
\tag{12}
\]
The averaged cap source `d^(-1)sum lambda_i mu|H_i` is dominated by the original source, has mass `t_0`, base mean j, and continuous centroid `c/t_0`. Its constituent centroids have covariance `A^2/(d t_0^2)`.

The integer coefficients have not vanished. Positive-part subadditivity only gives the valid further bound
\[
 \int\left(\sum_i\lambda_i a_i\cdot(z-j)\right)_+d\mu\le d.
\]
There is also an exact coverage identity at the anchor:
\[
 \sum_i\lambda_i L_i(j,x)=0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^d.
\]
Since all retained weights are positive, it is impossible for every margin to be negative or for every margin to be positive. Hence both these caps and their opposite closed halfspaces cover the entire anchor space. At another base z their weighted margin is exactly `(sum lambda_i a_i).(z-j)`. The cap masses remain t_0, which is not asserted to meet the OC budget. No step identifies these balanced cap sources with arbitrary caps through `c/t_0`, and no depth guarantee is concluded.

## 7. Exact checks: the real maximum, integer true centroids, and sharp parity count

Let `g=(g_z,g_x)` be the true full centroid of the original source. Complementation of densities gives the exact identity
\[
 Q(M-t,Mg_z-v)=Mg_x-Q(t,v).
\tag{13}
\]
Reflection and translation preserve John volume. Thus the two constraint pairs on the left and right have the same John radius. Their midpoint is always
\[
 b_*=(M/2,Mg_z/2).
\]
If a pair differs from b_*, strict concavity (6) makes the radius at b_* strictly larger. Hence b_* is the **unique global maximum over all real constraint pairs**.

In particular, if the true integer-coordinate centroid `g_z` is itself integral, the integer-base problem also has the unique maximizer `j=g_z`, `t=M/2`. At this pair (13) makes the raw moment body centrally symmetric about `Mg_x/2`; uniqueness of the maximum-volume ellipsoid makes its center that point. Dividing its center by t therefore gives exactly the original full centroid g. This is a geometric identification, and only implies whatever depth bound for that true centroid has separately been proved.

Finally the count `2^n` in (3) is sharp. For the product body `[0,1]^n x K` with one positive continuous convex body K, the only feasible integer bases are its binary vertices. Base balance at an extreme vertex confines every source to that single fiber. All these identical fibers consequently have the same maximal raw John radius, uniquely at source mass `|K|/2` by complementation and strict concavity. Thus all `2^n` integer bases maximize. The case `n=0` has its single maximizing base.

# Raw moment John maxima: attainment, strict interpolation, empty lattice hull, and mass stationarity

This is a theorem about a geometric source body. It does not assert that its John center has any halfspace-depth guarantee. Indeed `candidate e16770c76630ebf6` disproves such a selector inference already for intervals.

- 1. Definitions and conclusions
- 2. Compactness and the unique indicator support source, including boundary constraints
- 3. Strict interpolation of raw moment bodies
- 4. Positive attained maxima and harmonic interpolation of bases
